extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of philosophy of science and scientific method; scientific inquirers interested in explanation and theory formation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating scientific explanations: how laws of nature should be resolved, subsumed, and verified by induction, deduction, and observation, with examples from physics, chemistry, and physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method (Induction, Ratiocination, Verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method is constituted by Induction, Ratiocination, and Verification; these three parts together are the method by which the human mind attains its most conspicuous triumphs in the investigation of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction to gather observed uniformities, ratiocination (deduction) to derive consequences and relations, and verification (experiment/observation) to confirm deductions. The text credits this three-part method with enabling simple laws to account for vast phenomena (example: celestial motions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation as Deduction from More General Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A law or uniformity in nature is said to be explained when another law or laws are pointed out, of which that law itself is but a case, and from which it could be deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation should show that the target law is a particular instance of a more general law (not merely a verbal account). Example: explaining planetary motion by laws of rectilineal motion and gravitation so the complex law follows by deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution into Separate Causes plus Collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: When the law of an effect of combined causes is resolved, it must be resolved into the separate laws of the causes, together with the fact of their co-existence (collocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate explanation must include both: (a) the simpler laws governing each contributing cause, and (b) evidence that those causes coexist in the circumstances considered (their relative amount/proportions). Example: the law of planetary motion requires laws of rectilineal motion and centripetal force and the fact that both act in celestial regions in certain proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of Intermediate Links (Remote Cause → Proximate Cause → Effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law connecting two non-proximate links may be resolved by detecting an intermediate link: A seemed the cause of C, but A may be the cause of B, and B the cause of C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek intermediate phenomena that mediate remote causal sequences (e.g., touch → nerve change → sensation). Finding such links makes the explanation more general and indicates where to study limitations and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for More General and More Certain Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sequence is resolved into other laws, the latter are always laws more general than itself and, in the first two modes, they are also more to be relied on (more universally true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing explanations that reduce complex regularities to simpler, more general laws increases certainty and reduces susceptibility to exceptions. Use resolution to increase the generality and reliability of theoretical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit Accounting for Negative Conditions and Limits
rubrics_metrics.description: All laws of causation are liable to be counteracted or frustrated by the non-fulfillment of some negative condition; complex laws are subject to the negative conditions which attach to all the simpler causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good explanation must identify conditions under which the law may fail (negative conditions) and thereby delimit the law's applicability. Example: a complex combination can fail if any single contributing tendency is defeated (rust in a machine preventing expected joint effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that Complex Laws Are Less General and More Fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of a complex effect is less general than the laws of the single causes composing it, and more liable to be unfulfilled, because any contingency defeating a component defeats the complex law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer analysing phenomena into simpler component laws rather than treating complex regularities as fundamental; this aids robustness and identification of contingencies that could falsify the complex law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsumption / Unification under a More General Law
rubrics_metrics.description: A third mode of explanation is the subsumption of one law under another, or gathering several laws into one more general law which includes them all (e.g., terrestrial gravity and planetary attraction under gravitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unify similar phenomena by showing quantitative as well as qualitative identity so they are demonstrably cases of a single general law. This often requires combining observations from different classes of cases (terrestrial and celestial) to eliminate contingent circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of Multiple Independent Sets of Observations for General Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To arrive at laws which hold under an immense variety of circumstances (independent of space/time), requires many distinct sets of experiments or observations, conducted at different times and by different people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish general laws by accumulating independent lines of evidence across differing conditions and observers; partial laws from separate domains can be combined to form a universal law (example: combining terrestrial and celestial observations to infer universal gravitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation Does Not 'Cause' the Partial Law but Shows It as a Case
rubrics_metrics.description: In scientific explanation, saying one law 'accounts for' another means assigning other laws more general, together with collocations, from which the partial law follows; it is not correct to say the general law 'causes' the partial one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language that reifies general laws as causal agents of particular phenomena; instead present deductive derivation and collocations that make the partial law a case of the general one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Deduction to Extend Science and Determine Conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: By resolving laws into other laws, their range is extended since the laws thus resolved may thenceforth be deduced demonstratively from the laws they are resolved into.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce explanations that yield deductive consequences, enabling determination of conditions and predictions. Good explanations should enable further deductions and testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for New Instances by Applying Established Laws' Conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law has been brought to light, it is important to examine all cases which present the conditions necessary for bringing that law into action; this is fertile for demonstrations of special laws previously unsuspected and explanations of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively look for fresh instances matching the law's conditions (e.g., Faraday: where conductor moves at right angles to magnetic flux, expect electricity). Use established mechanistic conditions to predict and discover new phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collocations as Essential Ingredients of Explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolving complex laws, the collocations — the existence of certain agents or powers in certain circumstances of place and time — are as essential as the simpler causal laws themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation must document not only the governing laws but also that the relevant agents/powers are present in the situations considered (e.g., relative amounts/proportions of forces; presence of membranes in osmose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution Produces Laws of Greater Scope Which Point to Where Exceptions Will Occur
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sequence A→C is shown to depend on an intermediate B, the resolution shows that any failures of A→C are most likely to be found by studying B's effects or conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the structure of resolved laws to guide empirical searches for exceptions and boundary conditions: focus on intermediate phenomena to locate limitations of broader generalizations.
